content: The registers for maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH) services are generally cross-sectional in design, which means they are not suitable for longitudinal follow-up of pregnant and postpartum patients. In contrast, the antiretroviral therapy (ART) register is designed to allow for the observation of patient outcomes at various points during treatment. This is achieved by referencing specific patient cards or electronic medical records (EMRs) to understand the progression of events, such as a patient being recorded as deceased three months after initiating ART. Web Annex K provides a generic ART register template and includes a list of patients who are unable or unwilling to start ART shortly after an HIV diagnosis, along with the reasons for the delay. The updated ART register contains 20 rows, with each row representing one patient. Each row is further divided into two sub-rows: a white row for recording follow-up status and a grey row for additional details such as pregnancy or breastfeeding status for women of reproductive age, or enrollment in differentiated service delivery (DSD) ART models. The first page of the register captures demographic information, ART initiation status, key co-treatments, pregnancies, and regimen changes. This information is recorded once and updated as necessary. Pages 2–6 are dedicated to monthly follow-up data for patients on ART, starting from the month of ART initiation (month 0) and continuing for up to 10 years (120 months). At each monthly follow-up, the patient’s ART status (e.g., regimen code, stopped treatment with reasons, lost to follow-up [LTFU], transferred out, or deceased) is recorded in the white row. The grey row captures pregnancy or breastfeeding status and/or enrollment in DSD ART models. Additionally, CD4 cell counts and viral load (VL) test dates and results are recorded at key intervals, such as 6, 12, and 24 months. The updated ART register includes several new features: Revised drug regimen codes to reflect newly recommended antiretroviral drugs (ARVs) and regimens for adults, adolescents, children, and infants. Inclusion of DSD ART model enrollment in follow-up status to track enrolled clients. Updates to treatment-limiting toxicities, including weight gain. Revised codes for tuberculosis preventive therapy (TPT). A new column for tracking fluconazole prophylaxis for individuals with advanced HIV disease. Two types of reports aggregate data from the ART register: cross-sectional and cohort reports. The cross-sectional report provides a snapshot of the cumulative and current numbers of people living with HIV who are in care and on ART, disaggregated by age and sex, on a quarterly to annual basis. This report is useful for monitoring service uptake over time and planning resource allocation. It can also help identify trends such as late ART initiation, which may guide targeted outreach efforts. The cohort analysis report aggregates data based on the month and year when individuals started ART. This allows for tracking key indicators along the HIV care and treatment cascade, such as retention on ART, mortality, treatment interruptions, and viral suppression at specific time points (e.g., 6 months, 1 year, 2 years). Cohort analysis is particularly valuable for identifying trends over time, such as early versus late mortality, increasing LTFU rates, or the timing of regimen switches to secondor third-line therapies. Both cross-sectional and cohort reports rely on the ART register as their primary data source. Community-based ART service providers play a critical role in linking clients to health facility services, distributing medications, providing psychosocial support, and monitoring adherence. Under the WHO’s 2021 DSD guidelines, clients may initiate ART outside of health facilities and have less frequent clinical visits and medication pickups. Community health workers and service providers are encouraged to routinely monitor and report on a standardized set of actions to ensure comprehensive patient management. This includes reconciling community-based monitoring tools with facility-based ART registers or electronic equivalents to maintain accurate and up-to-date records. The guidelines also emphasize the importance of integrating HIV services with other health services to ensure comprehensive patient care. High-quality individual-level data are essential for informed decision-making and improving patient outcomes. As countries work toward achieving the UNAIDS 95–95–95 targets, it is crucial to collect and report accurate data in real time to identify service delivery gaps and improve care quality. Data quality assessments (DQAs) should be institutionalized as part of the data management cycle to ensure the effective use of resources, accurate monitoring of progress, and evidence-based decision-making. Key dimensions of data quality include accuracy, reliability, completeness, timeliness, accessibility, relevance, and confidentiality. Patient monitoring systems must adhere to data protection and confidentiality frameworks to ensure that data are used solely for patient care and program management purposes. A systems approach to data quality improvement involves routine activities integrated into health information systems, such as building robust data systems and training human resources.
